preamble: Retraction of the close front vowel [i] to the central [ɨ] after a non-palatalized consonant. In Polish, Proto-Slavic *i became y after sz, ż, rz, cz, dż, c and dz once these consonants lost their softness (szyć 'to sew', czysty 'clean', przy 'at'). In Romanian, Latin ī was centralized to /ɨ/ (spelled â, î) after /r/: rīdet > râde 'laughs', rīvus > râu 'river'. Renwick (2012), adapting Petrucci (1999), states the rule as /i/ > /ɨ/ after /r/, parallel to e > ă after /r/ in reus > rău 'bad', which makes râu and rău a minimal pair. In Russian, /i/ is pronounced [ɨ] after hard consonants, also across a prefix or word boundary: имя [ˈimʲə] 'name' but без имени [bʲɪz ˈɨmʲɪnʲɪ] 'without a name'.

examples.note: The change followed the hardening of the palatal sibilants and affricates; the Podhale dialects keep i after s and z (the Podhale archaism).
Minimal pair with rău /rəw/ 'bad', from Latin reus, where e was centralized after /r/ in the same way.

examples.to: без имени [bʲɪz ˈɨmʲɪnʲɪ] 'without a name', безымянный [bʲɪzɨˈmʲanːɨj] 'nameless'

examples.note: The final /i/ follows hard /ɫ/; unstressed /a/ is reduced to [ɐ] separately (Moscow standard; St Petersburg [ʌ]).

In the five-vowel (Moscow school) analysis [ɨ] is the allophone of /i/ after hard consonants; the six-vowel analysis treats /ɨ/ as a separate phoneme. Since 1956 the spelling uses ы after Slavic prefixes (безымянный).
